name: Functional medicine detox

lead: Functional medicine detox refers to structured cleanse or detoxification programs offered by practitioners of functional medicine, a clinical approach founded in the early 1990s. Programs typically combine restricted eating, supplements and lab testing, with the aim of clearing supposed accumulated toxins.

People interested in appearance use these programs hoping for clearer skin, less puffiness, steadier energy and weight change. Reviews of detox diets generally report that evidence for toxin removal is lacking, and weight lost on short programs is typically regained.

paras: Practitioners generally order tests (for example for heavy metals or other markers), then recommend an elimination-style diet, supplements and sometimes sauna or other adjuncts over a period of weeks. Programs are individualised and vary widely between clinics.

Very restrictive diets can lead to nutritional deficiency, and prolonged fasting can be dangerous. Critics note that extensive testing can produce false positives that lead to anxiety and unnecessary treatment, and that relying on detox may delay care for real disease. Short, balanced programs are generally regarded as harmless by reviewers.

chain: Practitioner tests and prescribes a cleanse
Restricted diet and supplements for several weeks
Short-term weight and bloat change; hoped-for clearer skin and energy
angle.text: People use clinician-run detox programs hoping that removing perceived toxins will clear skin, reduce puffiness and improve energy. Short-term weight change from restrictive eating is the most commonly reported outcome; reviewers note it is typically regained.

lead: Functional medicine detox is the detoxification component of functional medicine, a clinical approach created by Jeffrey Bland, who founded the Institute for Functional Medicine in Washington State in the early 1990s; the institute became a registered non-profit in 2001.[1] Within this approach, practitioners offer cleanse programs built from dietary changes, supplements and laboratory testing.[1]

People pursue these programs for appearance-related reasons: hoping that clearing "toxins" will show up as clearer skin, a less bloated midsection, brighter eyes and more energy. Some also hope for fat loss, which a detox diet may produce temporarily.[2]

Researchers and medical bodies have commented on both functional medicine and detox practices. A 2015 review of detox diets found no compelling evidence for them in weight management or toxin elimination, and the Mayo Clinic has said there is little evidence they remove toxins.[2] In 2014 the American Academy of Family Physicians withdrew continuing-education credit for functional medicine courses, partly restoring it for overview classes in 2018.[1]

paras: Functional medicine uses a disease model built on "antecedents," "triggers" and "mediators," which practitioners combine into a treatment "matrix."[1] Detox protocols are one of its common offerings and are presented as a way to reduce the body's burden of environmental chemicals, heavy metals or metabolic by-products.[1]

Detoxification in the wider alternative-medicine sense takes many forms: juice or fasting regimens, colon cleansing, chelation therapy, dental amalgam removal and devices such as foot baths.[2] Proponents say everyday foods and the environment deliver additives, pesticides and preservatives that accumulate, and that dieting releases stored toxins that leave via the blood, skin, urine, feces and breath.[2]

The Institute for Functional Medicine was founded by Jeffrey Bland in the early 1990s as part of one of his companies, and Mark Hyman later joined its board and became a prominent promoter.[1] The broader idea of purging the body has a long history: doubts about purging emerged by the 1830s, a 19th-century autointoxication theory was challenged by a 1919 JAMA article, and detox ideas revived with the growth of alternative medicine in the 1970s.[2]

Surgical oncologist David Gorski has described functional medicine as poorly defined and as ordering expensive tests he considers generally unnecessary.[1] McGill's Jonathan Jarry has warned that testing many markers in many people produces false positives that can lead to anxiety and treatment.[1] Joe Pizzorno, a functional medicine figure, has claimed that 25 percent of people in the US have heavy metal poisoning needing detoxification; the Wikipedia article reports this contradicts scientific evidence.[1]

The UK groups Sense about Science and the British Dietetic Association criticised detox products in 2009, and Edzard Ernst argued in 2024 that detox amounts to medical fraud.[2] Proponents counter that individualised programs address patient concerns that conventional care leaves unaddressed.

Short detox diets are generally considered harmless unless they cause nutritional deficiency, and weight lost is typically regained afterward.[2] Prolonged fasting can be dangerous or fatal, and colon cleansing carries risks.[2] Reported cases include a 2005 death after a man chose detox over dialysis and a 2008 award of over 800,000 pounds to a woman who suffered brain damage on a detox diet.[2]

No studies found on functional medicine detox programs as a package. A 2015 review of detox diets generally, by Klein and Kiat, found no compelling evidence for weight management or toxin elimination.[2]

timeline.event: A JAMA article challenges autointoxication theory.[2]
Jeffrey Bland founds the Institute for Functional Medicine.[1]
